newsitem.title: USA: IMM currencies close sharply lower after Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: IMM currencies close sharply lower after Greenspan.

text.p: IMM currency futures closed sharply lower on heavy hedge fund selling after the dollar rallied out of ranges in a delayed reaction to Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony, traders and analysts said.
They said funds that had aggressively turned short against the dollar were forced to cover positions after the greenback rose through key resistance levels.
"I think a lot of people got hurt on this move," one currency futures trader said after currency futures, including the yen, broke down.
"Funds were really caught short," George Tzanetatos, vice president at Merrill Lynch, said. "They had sold the dollar with the expectation that its rally was easing."

He said hedge funds were particularly short below 1.68 spot, or $0.5958 March marks, and that shortcovering by funds would push the dollar to 1.70 and possibly the previous high of 1.7050 spot, or $0.5888 to $0.5871, in the near term.
A fall to $0.5871 would be a new contract low.
One floor trader said fund selling turned heavy when March marks fell through $0.5938, or 1.6855 spot, and $0.5930, or 1.6880, and when March yen fell through $0.008190, or 122.40.

"With the dollar over 122.00 spot yen and 1.69, the dollar is now going to go screaming higher," another trader said. The futures equivalents to 122.00 spot yen and 1.69 spot mark are $0.008217 in March yen and $0.5923 in March marks.
He said March yen is poised to test $0.008021, or 125.00, which would be a contract low. The current contract low is $0.008044.

March yen initially rose above a three-week high to $0.008296 after Greenspan's comments about the unsustainable pace of U.S. stocks sent the Dow Jones Industrial Average and other major indexes sharply lower.

Greenspan also said in remarks in the first leg of the Humphrey-Hawkins testimony that the Fed may pre-emptively raise U.S. rates. Any Fed tightening, he said, would not be as aggressive as in 1994. U.S. bonds sold off sharply.
The negative reaction in the U.S. asset markets pushed the dollar to the lower end of its corrective ranges, and gave most futures contracts a firm tone.
However, forex traders quickly interpreted Greenspan's remarks in a more positive light for the dollar.
"He underlined the strength of the U.S. economy," Tzanetatos said.
In addition, Tzanetatos said the lack of commentary on the dollar relieved some speculation that the Fed would step in and call for an end to the dollar's recent rally.

Mexican peso futures expanded losses as U.S. stocks continued to weaken, traders said. One trader said poor results of Cetes auction, coupled with political uncertainties stemming from the country's drug problems, weighed on the peso all day.

At the end of pit trade, yen up $0.000035 at $0.008214, marks down $0.0059 at $0.5927, Swiss francs down $0.0078 at $0.6778, sterling off $0.0014 at $1.6340, Can dollars off $0.0034 at $0.7325 and pesos were off $0.000800 at $0.127025.
